Key point: Use serial tracking for individually accountable units and quantity tracking for interchangeable stock.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
33. Q: What is a LOT, and why can one location contain several inventory records for the same good?
A: Show answer
A lot groups items of the same type, often from one production run or supplier shipment, so the enterprise can trace inventory back to its source. One INVENTORY ITEM is associated with one LOT in the chapter's model. If the same good at one facility comes from several lots, separate inventory-item records preserve that provenance and enable targeted investigation or recall.
Study instruction: Create a warehouse example containing the same product from two supplier lots. Show how a customer complaint about one lot can be traced without recalling unrelated stock.
Key point: Lot identity preserves provenance and supports targeted recalls.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
34. Q: How does the model represent inventory location at different levels of detail?
A: Show answer
FACILITY represents the physical site, such as a warehouse, plant, building, or office. CONTAINER represents a more detailed location within a facility, while CONTAINER TYPE classifies the container as a shelf, bin, drawer, barrel, room, or similar location. Inventory can be tracked at the facility level when finer location detail is unnecessary, or within a container when precise picking and storage control is needed.
Study instruction: Draw a facility with several containers of different types. Place serialized and non-serialized inventory at both facility and container levels, and identify when a container reference may be absent.
Key point: Separate the site from its internal storage locations.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
35. Q: Why does INVENTORY ITEM STATUS TYPE need to be separate from inventory quantity?
A: Show answer
Inventory status describes condition or usability, such as good, under repair, damaged, defective, or scrap. It is not the same as quantity on hand. Keeping status as a reference type allows the enterprise to classify stock consistently, while a separate status-history relationship with a status date can preserve changes over time for serialized items. This prevents damaged stock from being treated as available merely because it exists physically.
Study instruction: Define a status list and map each status to whether it is available for sale, repair, or disposal. Add a dated status history for a serialized asset.
Key point: Physical existence and operational availability are different inventory facts.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
36. Q: How does ITEM VARIANCE provide an audit trail for inventory differences?
A: Show answer
ITEM VARIANCE records differences discovered during physical counts or inspections, including the discovery date, quantity difference, and reason. A negative variance reduces the recorded on-hand quantity; a positive variance increases it. The reason and comment explain causes such as theft, shrinkage, damage, or an unknown discrepancy. This creates an audit trail for quantity changes that do not arise from ordinary inbound or outbound shipments.
Study instruction: Record one negative and one positive variance, including dates and reasons. Reconcile the resulting on-hand quantity and explain what evidence should be retained before posting an adjustment.
Key point: Inventory adjustments should be explainable, dated, and auditable.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description; Microsoft Learn: Count, Adjust, and Reclassify Inventory
37. Q: Why is PRICE COMPONENT a reusable entity?
A: Show answer
PRICE COMPONENT represents a component of a price, such as a base amount, discount, surcharge, or suggested price. The chapter names it generically so the same structure can support product pricing and other contexts, including agreement pricing. Reuse avoids building separate, structurally similar price tables for each commercial process while allowing each price component to carry its own applicability and validity rules.
Study instruction: Identify three business processes that use price components. Compare their shared attributes and any process-specific rules that should remain outside the common entity.
Key point: A reusable price-component structure can support several pricing contexts.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
38. Q: What are the two non-mutually exclusive subtype dimensions of PRICE COMPONENT?
A: Show answer
One subtype set describes the price component's effect: BASE PRICE establishes the starting amount, DISCOUNT COMPONENT reduces it, SURCHARGE COMPONENT adds charges, and MANUFACTURERS SUGGESTED PRICE records a reference price. A second set describes charging pattern: ONE TIME CHARGE, RECURRING CHARGE, or UTILIZATION CHARGE. The sets are non-mutually exclusive because a component can be classified along both dimensions.
Study instruction: Classify sample price records by both their effect on price and their charging pattern. Explain why a one-time surcharge and a recurring base charge need both dimensions.
Key point: Price effect and charging pattern answer different classification questions.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
39. Q: How should PRICE COMPONENT represent validity and monetary values?
A: Show answer
From-date and thru-date attributes define the period during which a component is valid. The chapter provides either a fixed price amount or a percentage value, but not both on the same component. A comment can explain the commercial reason, such as a promotional discount. The one-of-two value rule should be enforced through a database constraint or equivalent validation, not left to user convention.
Study instruction: Create a fixed surcharge, a percentage discount, and an expired promotion. Validate date boundaries and test that no record stores both amount and percentage.
Key point: A price component needs an effective period and one unambiguous value representation.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
40. Q: Why can a PRICE COMPONENT relate to PRODUCT, PRODUCT FEATURE, and ORGANIZATION?
A: Show answer
A price may apply to the product as a whole, to a feature in the context of a product, or to a feature independently. The organization relationship identifies whose price is being recorded, which is essential when the same product is sold by the enterprise, a supplier, or a competitor. This allows feature premiums and competitor prices to coexist without confusing their ownership or context.
Study instruction: Model a base product price, a colour-specific premium, and a competitor's price. Identify the product, feature, and organization references required for each record.
Key point: Price context must identify the offering, priced feature, and relevant organization.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
41. Q: Which pricing factors can determine a PRICE COMPONENT?
A: Show answer
The chapter identifies geographic boundary, party type, product category, quantity break, order value, and sale type as common pricing factors. These allow a component to depend on delivery region, buyer segment, product family, order quantity, total order value, or sales channel. The model keeps these relationships flexible because a pricing rule may use one factor or a combination of several factors.
Study instruction: Build a pricing matrix using at least three factors, such as region, customer type, and quantity. Identify which combinations should generate a distinct price component.
Key point: Pricing rules are contextual and may depend on combinations of business factors.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
42. Q: Why must the enterprise define precedence rules for overlapping base prices?
A: Show answer
A buyer may qualify for more than one base-price rule, such as a regional price and a special customer-type price. The data model can store both rules but cannot decide their precedence without an explicit business policy. The enterprise must determine which component wins, whether rules combine, and whether a sales representative may choose among them. Without this policy, the same order could be priced inconsistently by different applications or users.
Study instruction: Create a buyer who qualifies for two base-price rules. Write a deterministic precedence rule and test the result in at least two order scenarios.
Key point: Flexible pricing data requires explicit and consistently enforced rule precedence.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
43. Q: How should discount rules handle overlapping eligibility and promotions?
A: Show answer
Discount components may depend on party type, geography, quantity, product category, or combinations of these factors. Several discounts may apply to one order, so the enterprise must decide whether discounts stack, whether one overrides another, whether they apply sequentially or to the original base, and who has authority to select an eligible discount. The chapter's model can store the conditions, but the policy must be made explicit.
Study instruction: Design a promotion with a customer-type discount and a category discount. Specify whether both apply, their calculation order, validity dates, and the rule for conflicting promotions.
Key point: Discount eligibility and discount-combination policy must be modeled separately.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
44. Q: What is a SURCHARGE COMPONENT, and how can it be applied?
A: Show answer
A surcharge adds a charge to the base price. The chapter gives freight and additional mileage as examples and notes that surcharges are commonly dependent on geography, such as distance from the nearest warehouse. Separating surcharges from base prices makes the reason for the added amount visible and permits the enterprise to maintain distinct validity and applicability rules.
Study instruction: Model a delivery surcharge for an outlying region. Explain how it differs from increasing the product's base price and how the surcharge should appear on an order.
Key point: A surcharge is an explicit additional charge, not an unexplained change to base price.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
45. Q: How do ONE TIME, RECURRING, and UTILIZATION charges differ?
A: Show answer
A ONE TIME CHARGE is assessed once, commonly when a good is purchased. A RECURRING CHARGE repeats over a time frequency such as an hour, day, or month. A UTILIZATION CHARGE is based on consumption measured in a unit, such as a number of internet hits. Recurring charges therefore need a time-frequency measure, while utilization charges need a unit that measures usage.
Study instruction: Classify a hardware purchase fee, monthly service subscription, and usage-based hosting fee. Identify the frequency or usage unit required to calculate each charge.
Key point: Charging cadence must match the business event being measured.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
46. Q: How should international product pricing be represented?
A: Show answer
A PRICE COMPONENT can be associated with a CURRENCY MEASURE so that the amount is interpreted in a defined currency. The chapter also notes that currency conversion could be stored through relationships among units of measure if the enterprise chooses to capture it. In implementation, the currency of a quoted price must be explicit, and any exchange-rate conversion should preserve the rate and effective date used for comparison or settlement.
Study instruction: Create prices for the same product in two currencies. Specify how a reporting currency is selected and what exchange-rate date is needed for a reproducible comparison.
Key point: A monetary amount is incomplete without its currency context.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
47. Q: Why does the chapter emphasize estimated product costs instead of deriving every cost from historical transactions?
A: Show answer
Actual costs may be distributed across purchase orders, freight and shipment records, payroll and time sheets, equipment assignments, and overhead transactions. The chapter's ESTIMATED PRODUCT COST model instead allows analysts to enter forward-looking cost estimates that incorporate current market conditions and expected trends. Estimates complement actual data; they are not a substitute for transaction-level accounting or operational records.
Study instruction: List actual data sources for material, freight, labour, equipment, and overhead. Then prepare an estimated cost for a future period and explain why it may differ from historical actual cost.
Key point: Estimated costs support forward planning; actual costs remain distributed across transactions.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
48. Q: What types of cost are represented by COST COMPONENT TYPE?
A: Show answer
The model distinguishes estimated materials costs, estimated labour costs, and estimated other costs. Other costs may include manufacturing equipment, shrinkage, shipping, selling expenses such as commissions or brokerage, and administrative overhead. The structure allows several components to contribute to the estimated cost of one product or feature rather than forcing all cost into a single undifferentiated amount.
Study instruction: For a manufactured good, distributor item, and consulting service, list the cost components each organization should estimate. Explain which categories are common and which are business-specific.
Key point: A product's estimated cost is a structured collection of cost components.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
49. Q: Why do estimated product costs need effective dates and contextual dimensions?
A: Show answer
Costs can vary over time, geography, and organization. The model uses from-date and thru-date attributes to show when an estimate applies, and optional relationships to GEOGRAPHIC BOUNDARY and ORGANIZATION to distinguish locations or entities. For example, freight and overhead may differ between regions even when the anticipated purchase cost is the same. These dimensions make cost comparisons meaningful and support period-specific planning.
Study instruction: Create two cost estimates for the same product in different regions and periods. Identify the exact dimensions required to retrieve the correct estimate for a planned sale.
Key point: Cost estimates are valid for a context and period, not necessarily for all operations.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
50. Q: How should estimated cost components vary by business model?
A: Show answer
A distributor may emphasize acquisition cost, freight and handling, selling expense, and administration. A manufacturer may add raw materials, production labour, equipment usage, and manufacturing overhead. A service organization commonly emphasizes labour, selling costs, and administration. The model should therefore support configurable cost-component types rather than imposing one universal cost breakdown on every enterprise.
Study instruction: Prepare separate cost-component lists for a distributor, manufacturer, and consulting firm. Remove categories that do not reflect the organization's actual cost drivers and document the rationale.
Key point: Cost structure should reflect how the enterprise creates and delivers value.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
51. Q: Why does PRODUCT COMPONENT apply beyond manufacturing?
A: Show answer
PRODUCT COMPONENT records which products are combined into another product. Manufacturing is only one use: distributors may sell kits of individually saleable goods, and service organizations may bundle software, documentation, training, and consulting hours into one offering. A product can contain several components, and a component can be reused in many parent offerings. The structure therefore represents commercial packaging as well as physical assembly.
Study instruction: Design a bundle for a distributor and a package for a service provider. Identify parent products, component products, and any components that are also sold independently.
Key point: Product composition can represent kits, bundles, and service packages as well as manufactured assemblies.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description; Microsoft Learn: Bills of Materials and Formulas
52. Q: Which attributes make PRODUCT COMPONENT useful for time-dependent assemblies?
A: Show answer
The chapter identifies quantity used, from-date and thru-date, instructions, and comment. Quantity states how many units of a component are included. Effective dates preserve changes to a product's composition over time. Instructions describe assembly steps, while a separate INSTRUCTION entity may be added when detailed procedures are needed. This makes the component relationship operationally useful rather than merely descriptive.
Study instruction: Model a kit whose component quantity changes on a future date. Preserve the old and new compositions and decide whether assembly instructions need a separate entity.
Key point: Composition records need quantities, validity periods, and sufficient assembly guidance.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
53. Q: How does PRODUCT SUBSTITUTE represent alternative products?
A: Show answer
PRODUCT SUBSTITUTE identifies a product that may replace another product. The relationship can be many-to-many because one product may have several substitutes and one substitute may serve as an alternative for several products. Effective dates define when substitution is allowed, quantity supports equivalent replacement amounts, and comments can warn about quality or suitability limitations.
Study instruction: Create two substitution rules, including a case where one package replaces twelve individual units. Add a quality warning and test whether the rule is valid for an order date.
Key point: Substitution is a governed equivalence or replacement rule, not merely a product similarity label.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
54. Q: What does PRODUCT OBSOLESCENCE capture?
A: Show answer
PRODUCT OBSOLESCENCE records products that are about to be or have already been superseded by other products. The recursive many-to-many relationship allows one old product to be replaced by several newer products and one new product to supersede several older products. This is important when product lines consolidate, split, or move through successive software or hardware releases.
Study instruction: Map a product family in which two older offerings are replaced by one new release. Identify which relationships are one-to-many or many-to-many and what lifecycle dates should be retained.
Key point: Obsolescence records lineage between replaced and replacement offerings.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
55. Q: How does PRODUCT COMPLEMENT differ from PRODUCT SUBSTITUTE?
A: Show answer
A complement is a product that works well with another product and may be recommended alongside it, such as refill paper for a desk blotter. A substitute replaces another product when the preferred product is unavailable or unsuitable. Confusing the two can produce poor recommendations: complementary products increase the usefulness of the original item, while substitutes provide an alternative to it.
Study instruction: For ten product pairs, classify each relationship as complement or substitute and explain the customer's likely buying decision.
Key point: Complements are used together; substitutes can replace one another.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
56. Q: What business purpose does PRODUCT INCOMPATIBILITY serve?
A: Show answer
PRODUCT INCOMPATIBILITY records combinations that should not be used together, such as a refill that does not fit a particular pen. This information can be checked during product selection or order entry to prevent unsuitable sales and avoid customer dissatisfaction. The chapter notes that if many combinations are being tracked, a broader PRODUCT COMPATIBILITY relationship may be easier to maintain, with compatible combinations represented explicitly.
Study instruction: Create an order-validation example involving a product and an incompatible accessory. Decide whether a negative incompatibility list or positive compatibility list is easier to govern for the expected number of combinations.
Key point: Compatibility rules protect customers and operations from invalid product combinations.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
57. Q: When is the alternate PRODUCT ASSOCIATION supertype useful?
A: Show answer
The alternate model groups component, substitute, obsolescence, complement, and incompatibility relationships under a common PRODUCT ASSOCIATION supertype because they share structural patterns and common attributes. PRODUCT ASSOCIATION TYPE identifies the meaning of each relationship and allows additional association types to be introduced. This reduces duplicated structures, but it also requires careful type-specific validation so that a component rule is not interpreted as a substitute rule.
Study instruction: Compare the separate-entity model with a typed association supertype. List shared attributes, type-specific attributes, and integrity rules needed to prevent invalid relationship combinations.
Key point: A common association supertype improves extensibility when relationship structures genuinely share a pattern.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
58. Q: How does the chapter distinguish FINISHED GOOD, RAW MATERIAL, and SUBASSEMBLY?
A: Show answer
A FINISHED GOOD is ready to ship, although work may have been performed on it. A RAW MATERIAL is an unworked lowest-level component used to make another product and may itself be sold. A SUBASSEMBLY is partially completed and is generally neither sold to customers nor purchased from suppliers in the model's stated context. If the enterprise buys a partially completed item from a supplier without further work, the chapter treats it as a raw material from that enterprise's perspective.
Study instruction: Classify components from a manufacturing process and justify each subtype using the item's state and the work performed by the enterprise.
Key point: These subtypes describe a component's role and state in the enterprise's production process.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
59. Q: Why might an enterprise model PART separately from PRODUCT?
A: Show answer
PRODUCT represents the marketable offering, while PART represents a physical item. The same physical finished good can be marketed as different products for different customer segments or commercial circumstances, such as a residential versus business service offering that uses the same underlying physical line. A separate PART entity is especially useful when parts are operationally significant, as in assembly-line manufacturing, repair, or detailed bill-of-materials management.
Study instruction: Use one physical item marketed in two different ways. Identify which attributes belong to PART and which belong to each PRODUCT offering, and explain why a single entity could blur the distinction.
Key point: A physical item and the commercial offering built around it are not always the same thing.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description
60. Q: How should an enterprise choose between the integrated product model and the separate PART model?
A: Show answer
Use the simpler GOOD subtypes when raw materials, subassemblies, and finished goods can be managed adequately as product variants. Introduce PART when the physical components have substantial independent requirements. In the separate model, PART BOM records part-to-part composition, while PRODUCT COMPONENT represents marketing packages. Parts also need appropriate links to inventory, pricing, reorder guidelines, and supplier offerings. The choice should follow real operational distinctions, not a desire to add entities unnecessarily.
Study instruction: Evaluate a distributor, a repair organization, and an assembly-line manufacturer. Choose the simpler or separate PART model for each, then verify that inventory, costing, sourcing, replenishment, and package relationships remain representable.
Key point: Choose the model that reflects operational reality while keeping product identity, physical parts, and commercial packages distinct.
Source links: Wiley: Volume 1 Book Description; Microsoft Learn: Bills of Materials and Formulas
Rows: 60
Table 4
Ordering Products: Orders, Procurement, and Agreements
1. Q: What business problem does an order data model solve?
A: Show answer
It records the commitments through which parties obtain goods or services and preserves the commercial and operational facts needed to execute them. Those facts include what is being ordered, quantity, price, expected delivery or service date, responsible parties, destinations, payment responsibility, terms, status, and links to prior requirements, requests, quotes, and agreements. The model must support both the seller's view of a sales order and the buyer's view of a purchase order. It should also preserve enough detail to support later fulfillment, invoicing, monitoring, and audit activities without treating every line printed on a document as a separate business object.
Study instruction: Map the lifecycle of a representative transaction and list the information needed at order creation, approval, fulfillment, billing, and review.
Key point: An order is a business commitment involving products, parties, terms, and subsequent execution—not merely a form or document.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders GS1: Messages Provided by the GS1 XML EDI Standard
2. Q: What are the limitations of the traditional separate sales-order and purchase-order model?
A: Show answer
A conventional model connects a customer to sales orders and a supplier to purchase orders, with line items referring to products. It is easy to understand, but it often duplicates structures that are substantially the same. Separate structures can lead to duplicate validation, status, pricing, and term-processing logic. The model can also hide the internal organization that received a sales order or placed a purchase order by assuming that the enterprise itself is implicitly involved. It may therefore fail to represent subsidiaries, divisions, stores, brokers, or other parties participating in a transaction. A richer model makes the common transaction structure explicit and records the actual participants and roles.
Study instruction: Compare two separate order schemas and identify common attributes, rules, and processing routines that could be shared.
Key point: A simple customer-supplier model can conceal organizational complexity and duplicate common order capabilities.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders
3. Q: Why can sales orders and purchase orders be modeled as two perspectives of one ORDER concept?
A: Show answer
Both describe a commitment to obtain or provide specified goods or services. A seller records the transaction as a sales order; the buyer records the corresponding transaction as a purchase order. Their core facts—dates, items, quantities, prices, delivery expectations, parties, and terms—are largely parallel, although each side may capture additional information relevant to its own operations. For example, the seller may record sales-credit or commission information that the purchaser does not need. A shared ORDER supertype supports common processing while subtypes preserve attributes and relationships specific to the sales or purchasing perspective.
Study instruction: Create a comparison of sales-order and purchase-order attributes and mark each as common, seller-specific, or buyer-specific.
Key point: Share the common transaction structure while retaining subtype-specific business facts.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders
4. Q: How should ORDER and ORDER ITEM subtypes be used?
A: Show answer
ORDER is the common parent for SALES ORDER and PURCHASE ORDER. ORDER ITEM is the common parent for SALES ORDER ITEM and PURCHASE ORDER ITEM. This arrangement supports common attributes and behavior while allowing a subtype to hold facts that apply only to one transaction perspective. It also avoids defining separate, unrelated order structures merely because the buyer and seller use different names for their documents. The subtype design should reflect genuine differences in business rules, not simply differences in screen labels or document layouts.
Study instruction: For a proposed subtype, identify the attributes or relationships that cannot correctly be stored on the common parent and explain why.
Key point: Use supertypes for shared transaction facts and subtypes for meaningful perspective-specific facts.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
5. Q: What is the difference between an order date and an entry date?
A: Show answer
The order date records when the enterprise gave or received the order as a business event. The entry date records when the order was entered into the enterprise's information system. These dates may differ when an order is received by telephone, email, an intermediary, or another channel and entered later. Keeping both dates preserves the distinction between the commercial event and its administrative recording. That distinction can matter for service-level measurement, effective agreement pricing, approval timelines, and investigation of delayed data entry.
Study instruction: Model a transaction received on one date and entered on another; identify which date should drive each relevant business rule.
Key point: Do not use system-entry time as a substitute for the date the order was actually made or received.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle Procurement: Purchase Order Pricing
6. Q: What information belongs on an ORDER ITEM?
A: Show answer
An ORDER ITEM identifies the specific good, service, or product feature being ordered and records transaction-level details such as quantity, unit price, estimated delivery or service-fulfillment date, shipping instructions, comments, and a free-form item description where needed. Quantity is interpreted using the product's unit of measure: it may mean units of goods, hours, days, or another service measure. The item is the appropriate level for facts that can differ within one order, including a negotiated unit price, a delivery date, or a destination. Header-level facts should not be repeated on every item unless the business rule genuinely requires item-level variation.
Study instruction: Take a mixed order and classify each field as order-header data, order-item data, or a separately modeled related fact.
Key point: Store item-specific commercial and fulfillment facts at the item level.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders GS1 EDI Business Terms
7. Q: How can the model represent both goods and services in the same order?
A: Show answer
Goods and services can both be represented by ORDER ITEMs, with quantity interpreted according to the associated product's unit of measure. A goods item might have a quantity of 20 units, while a service item might have 40 hours or 3 days. The chapter therefore does not require separate goods-order and service-order subtypes: a single order may contain both a physical product and a service. A descriptive item field can also accommodate work or professional time that is not represented by a standard catalog product, while a richer work-effort relationship can be introduced where service execution must be tracked in detail.
Study instruction: Design one order containing equipment, installation, and hourly support; specify the unit of measure and fulfillment data for each item.
Key point: Goods and services can share an order structure when quantity and fulfillment are interpreted using the product or service definition.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders
8. Q: Why store an order item's unit price when product pricing can be calculated from price components?
A: Show answer
A product's standard price may be derived from base prices, discounts, surcharges, quantity breaks, geography, party characteristics, or promotions. The order's unit price nevertheless records the price actually agreed for that specific transaction. It can preserve a negotiated override of the calculated standard price and provides a transaction-specific value for extensions and later review. The model should retain the applicable pricing basis and any override rules so that users can distinguish a catalog price from a negotiated order price rather than silently replacing one with the other.
Study instruction: Work through an example in which a catalog price is adjusted by a discount and then overridden by a negotiated order price; identify which value is retained on the order.
Key point: A transaction price is a committed commercial fact, not always a simple derivation from the current product price.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle Procurement: Purchase Order Pricing
9. Q: Why use ORDER ITEM rather than ORDER LINE ITEM as the entity name?
A: Show answer
A printed order line may contain more than the product being ordered. It can include tax, freight estimates, notes, discounts, explanations, or other document presentation details. ORDER ITEM is intended to represent the business fact that a good, service, or feature has been ordered, independent of how the transaction is laid out on paper or on a screen. Adjustments and other non-product facts can be modeled separately and associated with the order or item they affect. This keeps the logical model focused on business meaning rather than the physical layout of a document.
Study instruction: Review a sample purchase-order form and separate ordered products from taxes, freight, notes, and other document lines.
Key point: Model the ordered thing as an item; do not equate every printed line with an ordered product.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
10. Q: How should optional product features selected for an order be represented?
A: Show answer
A product may have selectable features such as color, size, quality, software capability, or another variation. The order should record the options actually selected, especially when they affect the delivered configuration or price. Required features can often be obtained from the product definition, whereas optional selections need transaction-specific records. The chapter models a feature selection as an ORDER ITEM related to the ORDER ITEM for the base product through a recursive association. This makes it possible for two order items for the same product to carry different feature selections without confusing their configurations.
Study instruction: Model two units of the same product with different colors and optional upgrades; verify that each selection is attached to the correct ordered instance or item quantity.
Key point: Preserve optional configuration choices against the particular ordered product item they modify.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders
11. Q: Why is a recursive relationship useful for order-item features?
A: Show answer
A recursive relationship allows one ORDER ITEM to refer to another ORDER ITEM in the same entity. In this design, an item representing a selected product feature is associated with the item representing the product to which the feature belongs. This is preferable to attaching a feature only to a product identifier when the same product can appear on multiple order items with different options. The relationship preserves the context of the specific ordered instance and can support multiple features for one product item. Implementations should enforce that a feature item cannot be attached to an unrelated order or incompatible product configuration.
Study instruction: Draw the recursive association for two order items of the same product with different feature selections and state the integrity rules.
Key point: Feature selections belong to a particular ordered item, not merely to the product type in general.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
12. Q: Which parties may participate in an order, and why is one CUSTOMER or SUPPLIER reference insufficient?
A: Show answer
An order may involve a party placing it, a party taking it, a party receiving delivery, a party paying, a party receiving installation or setup, and people or organizations responsible for entry, approval, quality assurance, management, sales, or fulfillment. These roles may be performed by different organizations or people. A customer that places an order may not be the recipient, payer, user, or installation location. Likewise, a purchase order may involve a purchasing entity, supplier, bill-to purchaser, ship-to buyer, and internal approvers. Recording roles explicitly avoids treating the word customer or supplier as if it described every relationship in the transaction.
Study instruction: For a multi-site order, identify every participating party and assign each a business role before designing the relationships.
Key point: Party identity and party role are separate facts; one transaction can involve many parties in different capacities.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders
13. Q: Why should order contact mechanisms be modeled separately from party contact details?
A: Show answer
A party's master contact information contains addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and other mechanisms used for ongoing communication. An order may use a temporary or transaction-specific contact mechanism that should not become the party's default contact. The order may also be received through a channel when the identity of the placing party is not yet known, such as a web endpoint or anonymous contact channel. Modeling the party role and the order contact mechanism as independent facts allows the system to record one even when the other is unknown. The relationship to a party's master contact record may be useful, but should not be assumed in every case.
Study instruction: Compare a customer's registered address with a one-time delivery address and an anonymous web order channel; determine which facts belong to the party and which belong to the transaction.
Key point: Transaction contact details can be independent of a party's permanent contact profile.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). GS1 EDI Business Terms
14. Q: Who may place an order, and how can the model validate an agent or broker?
A: Show answer
The placing party may be an individual, an organization, or an agent acting for another party. The appropriate choice depends on the enterprise and transaction channel. Where an agent or broker places the order, the model can record the actual placing party and use the relevant PARTY RELATIONSHIP information to determine whether that party is authorized to act for the principal. This prevents the system from assuming that every contact who submits an order has authority to commit the customer. Authorization rules should be evaluated at the time and scope relevant to the transaction, with evidence retained where the business requires it.
Study instruction: Model an order placed by a broker for a customer and specify the relationship and authorization checks required before acceptance.
Key point: Record the party that actually placed the order and validate its authority separately.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
15. Q: Why record the party and organization that took or received an order?
A: Show answer
The order is received by a real party or organizational unit, not by an abstract enterprise-wide “us.” It may be taken by a subsidiary, division, department, store, supplier, service center, or online channel. Recording the receiving party supports responsibility assignment, internal reporting, operational routing, and identification of the channel that accepted the commitment. A related contact mechanism can record the phone number, email endpoint, website URL, or other channel used. For a web order, the model can therefore preserve both the internal organization responsible for receiving it and the web mechanism through which it arrived.
Study instruction: Trace orders received through a store, a call center, and a website; identify the receiving organization and channel for each.
Key point: Capture which organizational unit took the order and through which mechanism it was received.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). GS1: Messages Provided by the GS1 XML EDI Standard
16. Q: Why is the ship-to party and destination often recorded at ORDER ITEM level?
A: Show answer
Different items on one order may be delivered to different parties or locations. A retailer, for example, may order a large quantity and allocate separate item quantities to several regional stores. If ship-to were restricted to the order header, the transaction would have to be split into multiple orders even when the commercial commitment is one order. Item-level destinations also support services delivered at different locations. The destination relationship can be optional when a service is performed across an organization or has no single delivery address. The requested destination is captured before the actual shipment is known, because later shipments may consolidate items from different orders.
Study instruction: Design one order with three item destinations and show how the item-level allocation avoids duplicating the order header.
Key point: Put destination data at the lowest level where the business permits it to vary.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders
17. Q: Why should requested ship-to information be stored on the order rather than only on a later shipment?
A: Show answer
The requested destination is known when the order is created and can influence how later fulfillment is planned. A shipment may combine order items from several orders, so the shipment does not necessarily define the original requested destination for each item. If the destination existed only on the shipment, the enterprise could lose the customer's original delivery instruction before shipment consolidation is decided. The order item should therefore retain the requested ship-to party and contact mechanism, while the shipment records the actual movement and destination details used during fulfillment.
Study instruction: Follow two orders whose items are consolidated into one shipment; distinguish requested destinations from actual shipment data.
Key point: Preserve customer delivery intent on the order and actual dispatch facts on the shipment.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders GS1: Messages Provided by the GS1 XML EDI Standard
18. Q: What is the difference between bill-to party and bill-to contact mechanism?
A: Show answer
The bill-to party identifies the person or organization responsible for payment. The bill-to contact mechanism identifies where or how billing communications should be sent, such as a postal address or email address. These are separate facts: the payer may be a parent organization while invoices are routed to a shared service center or a designated email address. Confusing the payer with the invoice destination can lead to incorrect responsibility, delivery, and collection records. The model should preserve both facts and allow the relevant business rules to determine whether a particular order or item uses a different billing arrangement.
Study instruction: For a subsidiary purchase paid by a parent company, specify the payer and the invoice destination independently.
Key point: The party liable to pay and the address or channel used to send the bill are not the same data element.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders
19. Q: When should an installation party and installation location be modeled separately from ship-to?
A: Show answer
Installation or setup may occur at a location different from the delivery destination. Equipment can be shipped to a receiving dock and installed at a department's premises, or a service provider may need a named installation contact. If the enterprise needs to coordinate setup, repair, or installation, the order item can identify the installation customer or contact and the relevant contact mechanism. These facts should not be added indiscriminately: they are justified when installation responsibility or location is a real business requirement. Separating them prevents the ship-to address from being overloaded with a second operational meaning.
Study instruction: Analyze an equipment order delivered to a warehouse but installed at a branch; list the separate parties, locations, and contacts.
Key point: Delivery and installation are different business events and may have different parties and locations.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
20. Q: When should order roles be modeled with explicit party-role relationships rather than a generic ORDER ROLE structure?
A: Show answer
Explicit relationships such as BILL TO CUSTOMER and SHIP TO CUSTOMER make the model easier to read and can express stable cardinality rules directly. They are preferable when the role set and business rules are well understood and unlikely to change. A generic ORDER ROLE linked to an ORDER ROLE TYPE and PARTY is more adaptable when new roles may be added or the number of parties permitted in a role may change. The generic approach can reduce schema changes, but some constraints may then need to be enforced in application logic, stored procedures, or validation routines. The choice is a trade-off between explicitness and structural flexibility.
Study instruction: Evaluate whether a bill-to rule is stable or likely to evolve, then justify an explicit or generic design.
Key point: Prefer explicit role relationships for stable rules and generic role structures when role variation is expected.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
21. Q: How does the generic order-role model support both sales and purchase orders?
A: Show answer
Each ORDER can have one or more ORDER ROLE records, each linked to a PARTY and classified by ORDER ROLE TYPE. Role types can describe placing party, supplier, customer, bill-to purchaser, ship-to customer, salesperson, approver, or other participants without requiring a new database relationship for every role. ORDER ITEM ROLE records can similarly represent item-specific roles such as ship-to buyer, installer, or installation contact. This structure allows new roles and different role cardinalities to be introduced through reference data. It is useful when sales and purchase transactions share a common role framework but use different role labels or participants.
Study instruction: Define a role-type catalogue for a business that processes both sales and purchase orders, and identify which roles belong at header versus item level.
Key point: Generic role types let one transaction structure represent many party roles without schema redesign for each new role.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
22. Q: How should order contact mechanisms be classified in a flexible model?
A: Show answer
An ORDER may have multiple ORDER CONTACT MECHANISMS, and an ORDER ITEM may have multiple ORDER ITEM CONTACT MECHANISMS. A CONTACT MECHANISM PURPOSE TYPE classifies the purpose, such as placing, confirmation, taken via, bill-to, ship-to, or installation. The CONTACT MECHANISM stores the actual address, phone number, fax number, email address, URL, or other endpoint. Keeping purpose separate from the contact value allows the same mechanism type to be reused in different contexts and allows multiple mechanisms for a purpose when required. Validation should ensure that the selected mechanism is suitable for its purpose and level of association.
Study instruction: Create sample order and item contact records for placing, confirmation, billing, shipping, and installation purposes.
Key point: Store the contact value separately from the business purpose for which it is used.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). GS1 EDI Business Terms
23. Q: Why model ORDER ADJUSTMENT separately from ORDER ITEM?
A: Show answer
An order adjustment is not itself a good, service, or feature being purchased. Discounts, surcharges, sales tax, shipping and handling, fees, and miscellaneous charges alter the financial amount associated with an order or item. Treating each adjustment as an ORDER ITEM would blur the distinction between what was ordered and how its price is adjusted, and would require recursive relationships to link adjustment items to the products they affect. A separate ORDER ADJUSTMENT entity allows adjustments to be classified and related to either the entire ORDER or a specific ORDER ITEM without misrepresenting them as products.
Study instruction: Classify the components of an invoice preview as ordered items or adjustments and justify each classification.
Key point: Keep the purchased good or service distinct from charges and credits applied to it.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
24. Q: What types of order adjustments should a model accommodate?
A: Show answer
The chapter identifies discount adjustments, surcharge adjustments, sales tax, shipping and handling charges, fees, and miscellaneous charges. A discount or surcharge may be a fixed amount or percentage and may apply to the whole order or a particular item. Fees can represent processing, handling, or management charges. Miscellaneous charges provide a controlled place for exceptional amounts, such as a correction related to a prior order. An ORDER ADJUSTMENT TYPE catalogue can classify detailed adjustment categories. The design should also record the adjustment's basis, amount or rate, affected order or item, and any relevant calculation or approval information required by the enterprise.
Study instruction: Build a test order with a per-unit discount, order-wide discount, delivery surcharge, processing fee, and tax; identify the target and calculation basis of each.
Key point: An adjustment needs an explicit type, amount or rate, and scope of application.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
25. Q: How can a sales-tax lookup structure be modeled without embedding tax rules in order records?
A: Show answer
A lookup structure can maintain tax rates by geographic boundary and product category, because tax treatment may vary by location and by the type of product. A product category can also identify tax-exempt goods where applicable. The order adjustment records the tax actually applied to the transaction, while the lookup data supports the calculation. The model is a data structure, not a statement of the tax law. Real implementations must use the applicable jurisdiction's current tax rules, effective dates, exemptions, sourcing rules, and authoritative tax guidance. A generic percentage table alone is not sufficient to establish legal tax treatment.
Study instruction: Design a tax lookup with effective dates and geographic and product dimensions; list the jurisdiction-specific rules that must be verified before use.
Key point: Separate tax calculation reference data from the transaction's recorded tax amount, and validate tax treatment against the governing authority.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
26. Q: Why preserve order-status history instead of storing only the current status?
A: Show answer
An order may pass through several states, such as received, approved, placed on hold, or canceled. An ORDER STATUS record with a status datetime preserves when each transition occurred and supports audit, cycle-time measurement, and reconstruction of events. If the enterprise only needs the current state, a direct relationship to ORDER STATUS TYPE may be sufficient. The choice depends on whether historical transitions are needed for operations, compliance, dispute resolution, or analytics. If history is retained, the model should define how duplicate, reversed, or corrected status events are represented and how the current state is determined.
Study instruction: Model an order that is received, approved, put on hold, released, and canceled; identify the data needed to reconstruct its history.
Key point: Use dated status events when the history of an order's progress matters.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders
27. Q: Which fulfillment statuses may be derived rather than stored directly on an order?
A: Show answer
Some apparent order statuses can be derived from related operational records. The chapter notes that shipped, completed, and invoiced can be inferred through shipment items and invoice items, while backordered can be inferred through order-item associations. This avoids storing the same fact in multiple places and risking inconsistency. A physical implementation may nevertheless expose convenient status values for performance or user-interface purposes, provided they remain synchronized with the authoritative fulfillment records. The logical model should distinguish a genuine order-state event from a status that summarizes related shipment, invoice, or sourcing data.
Study instruction: For each proposed order status, identify whether it is an event recorded on the order or a conclusion derived from shipment, invoice, or procurement records.
Key point: Avoid redundant status facts when they can be reliably derived from authoritative related transactions.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders GS1: Messages Provided by the GS1 XML EDI Standard
28. Q: How should order terms be represented at header and item levels?
A: Show answer
ORDER TERM records the commercial conditions associated with an ORDER or an individual ORDER ITEM, with TERM TYPE defining the meaning of each term. Examples include delivery conditions, cancellation charges, refund or exchange restrictions, and penalties for late or non-performing service. Some terms apply to the entire transaction, while others apply only to one product or service item. A term's value must be interpreted according to its type; a percentage, date, duration, or descriptive clause cannot be treated as one generic value without context. Effective dates and references to the governing version may also be required in a production contract or order system.
Study instruction: Assign cancellation terms to an order and a non-performance penalty to one service item; explain why the scopes differ.
Key point: Model terms as typed conditions and attach each one at the level where it applies.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle Procurement: Blanket and Contract Purchase Agreements
29. Q: What is the purpose of ORDER ITEM ASSOCIATION?
A: Show answer
ORDER ITEM ASSOCIATION links one order item to another when the fulfillment or sourcing of one item depends on another. A common case is a distributor that accepts a sales order but does not have enough stock, so it creates one or more purchase order items to obtain the missing goods. The association records which purchase order items are intended to fulfill which sales order items. It supports many-to-many relationships: one purchase item can supply several sales items, and one sales item can be covered by purchase items from multiple suppliers. This is more precise than simply marking an entire order as backordered.
Study instruction: Trace a sales item split across two suppliers and a purchase item allocated to multiple customers; map the associations.
Key point: Use item-level associations to preserve the sourcing and fulfillment relationship across orders.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders
30. Q: When should a corresponding purchase-order number be stored instead of creating a full ORDER ITEM ASSOCIATION?
A: Show answer
A seller may need only the buyer's corresponding purchase-order identifier for reference, without needing to maintain the buyer's complete purchase-order details. In that case, the corresponding PO ID can be stored on the SALES ORDER ITEM. It belongs at item level because different items on one sales order may refer to different buyer purchase orders. A full ORDER ITEM ASSOCIATION is more appropriate when the enterprise needs to represent actual sourcing or fulfillment dependencies between sales and purchase order items. The identifier alone should not be mistaken for evidence that the two items have a detailed allocation relationship.
Study instruction: Compare a customer-provided PO reference with a distributor's internal replenishment PO; choose the appropriate data structure for each.
Key point: Store a reference number when only identification is needed; model an association when the relationship itself must be managed.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
31. Q: What is a REQUIREMENT in the order lifecycle?
A: Show answer
A REQUIREMENT represents a need that may lead to an order. It can capture a customer's need or an internal organizational need, and it may concern a product or a work activity. Some enterprises need to manage customer requirements before proposing a solution; others mainly track internal purchasing needs. Recording requirements makes it possible to connect the original need to subsequent requests, quotes, and order items, and to measure whether the commitment actually satisfies the need. A requirement is not itself an order: it expresses what is needed before the organization decides how to fulfill it.
Study instruction: Choose one customer need and one internal need and show how each could progress from initial capture to an order.
Key point: A requirement records the need that motivates a possible commitment; it does not mean that a purchase has already been made.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Acquisition.gov: FAR Subpart 15.2 — Solicitation and Receipt of Proposals and Information
32. Q: How can requirements be classified as customer, internal, product, or work requirements?
A: Show answer
A requirement may be a CUSTOMER REQUIREMENT or an INTERNAL REQUIREMENT, depending on whose need is being represented. It may also be a PRODUCT REQUIREMENT or a WORK REQUIREMENT, depending on whether the need concerns a product or an activity to be performed. These classifications describe different dimensions and should not be collapsed into a single mutually exclusive label unless the enterprise's rules require it. A product requirement may identify a specific PRODUCT, desired features, or both. A work requirement may describe a task such as repair, maintenance, installation, or a broader project that will later be decomposed or fulfilled by services.
Study instruction: Classify requirements for office supplies, customer system development, equipment repair, and internal facility maintenance.
Key point: Capture whose need it is and what kind of need it represents as distinct classification facts.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
33. Q: Why allow a REQUIREMENT to be composed of other REQUIREMENTs?
A: Show answer
A recursive requirement structure supports decomposition from a broad need into smaller, manageable needs. A requirement to clean an office regularly might be divided into hiring a cleaning service and procuring cleaning supplies. A project to develop a sales-analysis system might be decomposed into needs analysis, package selection, hardware and software selection, and implementation. The parent-child structure allows planning, responsibility assignment, budgeting, and fulfillment to occur at different levels of detail. The enterprise should define whether child requirements inherit dates, ownership, status, or budgets from the parent, or whether those facts must be maintained independently.
Study instruction: Decompose a high-level operational requirement into at least three child requirements and define the rules for status and budget roll-up.
Key point: Recursive requirements represent the hierarchy of a need without forcing every need into a flat list.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
34. Q: Which roles and statuses are useful for managing a requirement?
A: Show answer
REQUIREMENT ROLE can identify the owner, originator, manager, authorizer, and implementer, with each role linked to a PARTY and optionally bounded by from and thru dates. REQUIREMENT STATUS can preserve a history of states such as active, on hold, and inactive, with a timestamp for each status event. The requirement may also identify the facility where the need exists, such as a plant, warehouse, office, or room. Together, these structures make it possible to identify who is accountable, when responsibility applies, where the need must be fulfilled, and how the requirement has progressed over time.
Study instruction: Assign roles and status events to a facilities-repair requirement, including a change of manager and a temporary hold.
Key point: Requirement management needs ownership, authorization, location, and time-aware status information.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
35. Q: How should desired product features distinguish required from optional characteristics?
A: Show answer
A PRODUCT REQUIREMENT can identify a product and one or more DESIRED FEATURE records. An optional indicator distinguishes a preferred feature from a mandatory one. For example, a blue pen may be preferred but not essential, whereas a specified capacity or compatibility requirement may be mandatory. This distinction matters when evaluating quotes or proposals: a supplier's alternative may satisfy the mandatory need while failing to provide a preferred feature. The model should not assume that every desired feature is a hard acceptance criterion, and the evaluation process should make the treatment of optional features explicit.
Study instruction: Create a requirement with two mandatory features and one optional feature, then evaluate a proposed substitute product against it.
Key point: Record whether a desired feature is mandatory or optional so supplier responses can be assessed correctly.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Acquisition.gov: FAR Subpart 15.2 — Solicitation and Receipt of Proposals and Information
36. Q: Why is the relationship between REQUIREMENT and ORDER ITEM many-to-many?
A: Show answer
One requirement may be fulfilled by several order items, such as when a large need is sourced from different suppliers or delivered in stages. Conversely, one order item may satisfy several requirements when the enterprise combines similar needs into a single purchase. ORDER REQUIREMENT COMMITMENT resolves this many-to-many relationship and records the quantity allocated from an order item to a requirement. Without the allocation quantity, the enterprise could know that an order item is related to a requirement but not how much of the ordered quantity satisfies that need. This is important for partial fulfillment, budget control, and avoiding double allocation.
Study instruction: Model two requirements for 1,500 pencils each and one purchase item for 2,000 pencils; allocate the ordered quantity without exceeding it.
Key point: The associative commitment record explains how much of each order item fulfills each requirement.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
37. Q: What is a REQUEST, and how does it differ from a REQUIREMENT?
A: Show answer
A REQUIREMENT records the need; a REQUEST communicates a solicitation or inquiry intended to obtain information, bids, quotes, or proposals about how that need may be met. A request can be sent by the enterprise to prospective suppliers or received by the enterprise from a customer seeking an offer. The request therefore adds a communication and market-engagement stage to the lifecycle. It records the request date, response deadline, description, participants, and request items. A requirement can exist without a request, and the same requirement may be included in more than one request over time.
Study instruction: Draw a process in which an internal need is captured first and then sent to several suppliers for responses.
Key point: A requirement is the need; a request is the solicitation or inquiry about that need.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Acquisition.gov: FAR Subpart 15.2 — Solicitation and Receipt of Proposals and Information
38. Q: What are the differences among RFI, RFQ, and RFP in the chapter's request model?
A: Show answer
An RFI seeks preliminary information, often about supplier capabilities or market options, and may be used to screen potential respondents before a more formal solicitation. An RFQ asks for prices or bids for specified products or services. An RFP asks a supplier to propose a solution to a stated need and may require an approach, benefits, resources, schedule, and supporting justification rather than a simple price. The precise legal and procedural meaning of these instruments depends on the procurement regime and solicitation. In US federal contracting, FAR guidance treats RFIs as information-gathering instruments and describes RFPs as a means of communicating requirements and soliciting proposals; those rules should not be generalized to every private or public procurement setting.
Study instruction: Choose an RFI, RFQ, or RFP for three scenarios and explain what information the buyer expects to receive.
Key point: Select the request type according to whether the objective is market information, comparable pricing, or a proposed solution.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Acquisition.gov: FAR Subpart 15.2 — Solicitation and Receipt of Proposals and Information Acquisition.gov: FAR Part 12 — Commercial Products and Services
39. Q: Which parties and contact details should a REQUEST record?
A: Show answer
A request may have REQUEST ROLE records for the originator, preparer, manager, quality assurer, and other participants. Each role is linked to a PARTY and classified by REQUEST ROLE TYPE. For outgoing requests, RESPONDING PARTY records the suppliers or other parties invited to respond, and the contact mechanism records how the request was or will be sent. The date sent can be maintained for each responding party because different recipients may receive the request at different times. Incoming requests commonly have one responding party—the part of the enterprise expected to prepare the response—so the model should accommodate both directions of communication.
Study instruction: Model one RFP sent to three suppliers by different channels and identify the originator, preparer, recipients, and sent dates.
Key point: Separate the request's internal roles from the external parties expected to respond.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Acquisition.gov: FAR Subpart 15.2 — Solicitation and Receipt of Proposals and Information
40. Q: What information belongs on a REQUEST ITEM?
A: Show answer
A REQUEST ITEM describes an individual part of the solicitation and may record quantity, required-by date, maximum acceptable amount, and a product reference or free-form description. A request for a known product can identify the PRODUCT directly. A request for a proposed solution to a problem may instead use a description of the problem or desired outcome. The maximum amount can communicate a price ceiling beyond which the response will not be considered. The item can also be associated with one or more REQUIREMENTs so the enterprise can trace why the request was issued and which needs it addresses.
Study instruction: Create an RFQ item for a catalog product and an RFP item for a repair outcome; identify the appropriate product and description fields.
Key point: A request item can specify a known product or describe a problem for which a solution is sought.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Acquisition.gov: FAR Subpart 15.2 — Solicitation and Receipt of Proposals and Information
41. Q: Why is REQUIREMENT REQUEST needed as an associative entity?
A: Show answer
A single requirement may be included in multiple requests, such as an RFI followed by an RFQ or a later competitive solicitation. One request item may also combine several requirements, such as one request to repair equipment from multiple departments. This is a many-to-many relationship, so REQUIREMENT REQUEST records the relationship without forcing either side to be unique. A simpler direct relationship from REQUEST to REQUIREMENT may be sufficient only when the enterprise can guarantee that requirements will not be reused across multiple request items and that multiple requirements will not be combined into one request item.
Study instruction: Build a matrix of requirements and request items for a staged procurement and test whether a direct one-to-one design can represent it.
Key point: Use the associative entity when requests and requirements can be reused or combined in both directions.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
42. Q: What is a QUOTE in relation to a REQUEST?
A: Show answer
A QUOTE is a response to a request and may be called a bid or proposal depending on the enterprise and procurement context. It provides the price, proposed product or service, and terms offered in response to the request. A quote records the issuing party and receiving party, along with other roles such as reviewer or approver. A request may receive many quotes from competing suppliers, but each quote item should answer a specific request item. The quote therefore preserves the supplier's response rather than simply copying the original request, which is important when the proposed solution differs from what was requested.
Study instruction: Link a request issued to three suppliers to three separate quote records and identify the issuer and recipient of each.
Key point: A quote is a party's response to a particular request, not just another name for the request itself.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Acquisition.gov: FAR Subpart 15.2 — Solicitation and Receipt of Proposals and Information
43. Q: What is the difference between a PROPOSAL and a PRODUCT QUOTE?
A: Show answer
A PROPOSAL is generally more elaborate and may describe the supplier's approach, understanding of the need, benefits, cost justification, resources, and delivery method. A PRODUCT QUOTE is typically narrower and records prices and terms for specified products. The QUOTE supertype can support both, with subtypes reflecting the amount and kind of response information required. Enterprises may use additional quote types such as bids or offers, but those labels should be defined according to the organization's process and legal environment rather than assumed to have identical meaning everywhere.
Study instruction: Compare a proposal for a managed repair service with a product quote for office supplies; identify the information each must contain.
Key point: Use quote subtypes to distinguish a solution-oriented proposal from a product-and-price response.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Acquisition.gov: FAR Subpart 15.2 — Solicitation and Receipt of Proposals and Information
44. Q: Why must a QUOTE ITEM link to a REQUEST ITEM and also identify the quoted product or service?
A: Show answer
The relationship to REQUEST ITEM establishes exactly which solicitation item the response addresses. The quoted product should also be recorded because a supplier may offer a more specific or alternative product than the one requested. For example, a request may ask for a generic number-two pencil while the supplier quotes a branded model with additional characteristics. If the quoted product were inferred only by following the link to the request item, the model would incorrectly assume that the supplier offered exactly what was requested. A quote item can also describe a work effort when the response is for a service solution rather than a catalog product.
Study instruction: Model a request for a generic product and a quote for a specific substitute; explain why both product references must be retained.
Key point: Preserve both the requested item and the actual item or solution offered.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
45. Q: How can QUOTE ITEMs be related to orders after a quote is accepted?
A: Show answer
A quote item may lead to one or more ORDER ITEMs because the quoted offer may be used for several orders or releases. An ORDER ITEM will generally be based on no more than one quote item, while a quote item can support multiple resulting order items. This preserves traceability from the supplier's offer to the commitments actually placed. If an order item is assembled from several distinct quoted sources, the enterprise should define whether it must split the order item or use a more detailed allocation structure. The relationship should not imply acceptance merely because a quote exists; the acceptance decision and resulting order remain separate business events.
Study instruction: Trace one accepted quote item into two orders and identify how the quoted price and terms are carried forward or overridden.
Key point: Keep the quote-to-order lineage so the enterprise can explain which offer supported each commitment.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied). Oracle: Overview of Managing Sales Orders
46. Q: Why can quote terms apply at both QUOTE and QUOTE ITEM level?
A: Show answer
Some conditions govern the entire offer, while others apply only to a particular product or service. A quote-wide term might require the customer to provide a central point of contact; a quote-item term might state that freight will be charged at actual cost for one furniture item. QUOTE TERM can associate typed terms with either the quote or an individual quote item. The TERM TYPE catalogue supplies the meaning of each term. This prevents item-specific conditions from being incorrectly applied to every item and allows common conditions to be recorded once at the quote level.
Study instruction: Separate a proposal-wide validity condition from an item-specific freight condition and identify their proper associations.
Key point: Apply quote terms at the level where their obligations and exceptions actually operate.
Source links: Primary source: Len Silverston, The Data Model Resource Book, Volume 1, “Ordering Products” (Chapter 4 source file supplied).
47. Q: How does an AGREEMENT differ from an ORDER?
A: Show answer
An ORDER is generally a transaction-specific commitment to buy or provide goods or services. An AGREEMENT establishes terms and conditions that govern how parties will conduct business over a period of time and may influence multiple orders. It can define commercial roles, product scope, pricing programs, exclusivity, renewal, termination, indemnification, and other legal or financial conditions. An agreement may exist before any order is placed, and an order may be governed by one or more applicable agreements. The model should therefore represent agreements as distinct business objects rather than treating them as unusually large orders.
Study instruction: Compare a one-time purchase order with a two-year supplier agreement and identify which facts belong to each record.
